extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament, policymakers, and the politically engaged public (late-18th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Abstract/record of Edmund Burke's speech in the House of Commons on the army estimates (Feb 9, 1790), arguing principles for judging standing forces, foreign policy toward France, and the limits of reform. The text sets out normative standards about confidence in ministers, balance of power, military discipline, and the political effects of foreign example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence vs. jealousy in ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Confidence might become a vice, and jealousy a virtue... That confidence, of all public virtues, was the most dangerous, and jealousy in an House of Commons, of all public vices, the most tolerable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidence in ministers should be conditional and subject to responsibility; where ministers cannot disclose particulars for necessary secrecy, confidence may be proper, but otherwise Parliament should exercise jealousy—especially when proposed measures (e.g., increases in peace establishments) are not clearly supported by visible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of army size depends on balance of power
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the annual Mutiny Bill the annual army was declared to be for the purpose of preserving the balance of power in Europe. The propriety of its being larger or smaller depended, therefore, upon the true state of that balance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions to increase the peace establishment must be justified by the actual state of the European balance of power; absent such justification, Parliament ought to resist enlargement of the forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess foreign states by strength, not form of government
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was to her strength, not to her form of government, which we were to attend; because republics, as well as monarchies, were susceptible of ambition, jealousy, and anger, the usual causes of war."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threat assessment should focus on material capability and intent rather than whether a state is a republic or monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not increase military/financial burdens while rival is weak
rubrics_metrics.description: "If, while France continued in this swoon, we should go on increasing our expenses, we should certainly make ourselves less a match for her when it became our concern to arm."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary peacetime expansion of military expenditure that erodes capacity relative to a rival when it recovers; policy should account for future recovery of adversaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware contagion of foreign example (anarchy/atheism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger from France lies not only in force but in example: the present danger was 'a danger from anarchy' and 'on the side of religion, the danger...from atheism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how foreign political and moral examples can influence domestic attitudes and institutions; guard against domestic imitation of the most corrosive aspects of foreign movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain military discipline under single authority
rubrics_metrics.description: "Armies cannot exist under a divided command... We have put them under a single authority, with a simple (our common) oath of fidelity; and we keep the whole under our annual inspection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standing army requires unified command and clear chains of responsibility; divided or competing military authorities (e.g., municipal armies alongside crown armies) risk mutiny and breakdown of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing armies are dangerous to liberty; undisciplined armies ruin society
rubrics_metrics.description: "An armed disciplined body is, in its essence, dangerous to liberty; undisciplined, it is ruinous to society. Its component parts are in the latter case neither good citizens nor good soldiers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the double peril of standing forces: maintain discipline, accountability, and oversight (e.g., annual inspection and oaths) to mitigate threats to liberty and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformation must preserve the contexture of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anything which unnecessarily tore to pieces the contexture of the state not only prevented all real reformation, but introduced evils which would call, but perhaps call in vain, for new reformation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate measured, conservative reform that corrects abuses without destroying the institutional balances and counterpoises that sustain the state; avoid wholesale dismantling that creates greater evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confiscation of established property (e.g., Church) undermines national prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: They 'laid the axe to the root of all property, and consequently of all national prosperity, by the principles they established and the example they set, in confiscating all the possessions of the Church.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that destroy property rights and confiscate longstanding institutions have severe economic and social consequences and should be judged accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldiers should remain disciplined soldiers, not mutineer citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of French troops: 'These soldiers were not citizens, but base, hireling mutineers... common soldiers deserting from their officers, to join a furious, licentious populace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutional arrangements that blur the soldier/citizen distinction in ways that encourage desertion from command, sedition, or use of military force for factional ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive governmental secrecy is harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote observation: 'The keeping of such secrets too long has been one cause of the Carnatic war, and of the ruin of our affairs in India.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit secrecy; prolonged concealment of important designs and information can produce mistrust, mismanagement, and geopolitical disasters.
